Good morning. It is Wednesday, May 20th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: Today has one of those mixes where foreign policy, rates, school budgets, AI policy, and your local forecast all end up connected by cost and follow-through.

HOST: We start with the story that is still setting the tone for oil, inflation pressure, and market nerves. After Monday's pause, President Trump said Tuesday that the United States may need to strike Iran again and that he had been about an hour away from making that decision before pulling back. That is the clearest sign yet that yesterday's apparent cooling was not a durable reset. It was a delay.

HOST: This matters because the practical question is no longer whether military pressure remains on the table. It obviously does. The question now is whether the White House can get enough out of renewed diplomacy to keep this from turning back into another direct escalation cycle before markets, gas prices, and consumer sentiment absorb a fresh hit. When the president says he nearly approved another strike, that tells you the risk premium on energy does not disappear just because crude backs off for a few hours.

COHOST: So the continuity from yesterday still holds, but the language got harder, not softer.

HOST: Exactly. The fresh development is that the pause now looks more fragile than it did twenty-four hours ago. If you are trying to understand why bond yields are still elevated and why investors look more defensive than confident, this is a big part of it. Even when oil eases intraday, traders are still pricing the possibility that one new military turn could shove energy higher again and keep inflation hotter for longer.

HOST: The second continuing national story is Taiwan, and this one also advanced in a meaningful way overnight. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te said Wednesday that if he had the chance to speak directly with Trump, he would stress that peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are crucial for global security and that continued U.S. arms purchases are essential to preserve that stability. That is a direct answer to the uncertainty created after the Trump-Xi summit, when Trump suggested further Taiwan arms sales could be treated as a negotiating chip.

COHOST: Taipei is not being subtle here. It is trying to drag the conversation back from transaction to deterrence.

HOST: That is the right read. Lai's message is basically that Taiwan is increasing defense spending because the threat is real, not because it wants symbolism or brinkmanship. So this story remains active because the White House still has not offered the kind of plain, unmistakable clarification that markets, allies, and Beijing would all understand the same way. Until that happens, Taiwan risk stays tied to semiconductor supply, manufacturing confidence, shipping costs, and the larger question of whether American deterrence is being priced as firm policy or improvised leverage.

HOST: The third national story stays in Washington, where Senate Republicans are still trying to move their immigration enforcement package while dealing with the limits of reconciliation and some open resistance inside their own conference. The newest pressure point is the White House push for one billion dollars in security additions for the White House campus and the president's new ballroom. Associated Press reports that Republicans are revising the proposal after the Senate parliamentarian said it did not fit reconciliation rules, and several Republican senators are already questioning whether that funding should survive at all.

COHOST: So the fresh angle is not just procedure. It is coalition strain.

HOST: Right. The story here is that even after repeated revisions, Republicans are still not at the point where they can stop negotiating and simply pass the thing. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday that it will come down to what they have the votes to pass. That is a polite way of saying the package is still unsettled. If more pieces get challenged or stripped, the broader takeaway will be that the party's procedural lane is narrower than its message discipline suggests.

HOST: The fourth national story is political rather than legislative, but it matters because it explains the mood inside the Republican Party this morning. Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein defeated Representative Thomas Massie in Kentucky's Republican primary on Tuesday, ending the career of one of the party's most independent and openly defiant House members. The result is bigger than one district. It is another warning shot to anyone in the GOP who thinks local strength or ideological distinctiveness is enough to survive a direct fight with Trump.

COHOST: Massie was not a marginal figure. If he can be taken out, the message lands everywhere else.

HOST: That is why this deserves attention today. Massie had a deep political identity of his own and a long record of bucking leadership. But the AP's reporting makes clear that Trump and his allies turned the race into a demonstration of presidential muscle, and they won. Pair that with the president's recent pressure on other Republican dissenters, and the lesson is that intraparty resistance is getting more expensive and more dangerous. That matters for Senate behavior, House behavior, and how much open disagreement you should expect the next time a big foreign policy or spending vote arrives.

HOST: Turning to Columbus, the clearest local development in the last twenty-four hours is the Columbus City Schools board vote to cut 299 positions as part of a plan to reduce next school year's budget by 50 million dollars. WOSU reports most of the eliminated positions are open roles, and the district says the cuts are concentrated in building substitutes and attendance program specialists. Superintendent Angela Chapman said the reductions were designed to stay as far from the classroom as possible, but she also acknowledged the district will still be trying to meet student needs with fewer hands.

COHOST: This is one of those stories where officials can say classroom instruction was protected, but families and staff still feel the loss through everything around the classroom.

HOST: Exactly. That is the practical lens. The district says it has already cut contracts, travel, training, administrative roles, and buildings. Now it is cutting nearly 300 more positions to finish the budget math. So the watch is what this means operationally once summer planning turns into the actual school year. Do attendance problems worsen? Does building coverage get thinner? Does the state funding argument create any immediate pressure in Columbus or at the Statehouse? This is not just a budget story anymore. It is a service-delivery story.

HOST: The next local and housing story sits right at the intersection of borrowing costs and buyer strain. Freddie Mac's latest weekly benchmark, released May 14th, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.36 percent. That is only a hair below the prior week, which tells you relief remains limited. At the same time, WOSU's latest central Ohio housing update shows April closed sales down 13.6 percent from a year earlier to 2,202, while the median sales price rose 8.3 percent year over year to 346,500 dollars.

COHOST: Fewer closings and higher prices is not a market that feels easier just because inventory is improving.

HOST: Correct. The cleaner way to say it is that central Ohio housing is normalizing in tempo, not becoming affordable in any broad sense. More inventory helps with choice. It does not magically solve payment shock when mortgage rates are still in the mid-sixes and household budgets are getting squeezed by food, insurance, and energy costs. So the fresh takeaway this morning is that the buyer bottleneck remains cost, not demand. People still want homes. The monthly payment still keeps too many of them from acting comfortably.

HOST: That brings us to AI and technology, where a fresh Washington move could have very real implications here in Central Ohio. Axios reports that the White House is preparing an executive order that could come as soon as this week and would create a voluntary framework for advanced AI developers to share new models with the government before public release. In plain English, the administration appears to be moving from broad talk about AI safety toward a more formal pre-release review structure for frontier systems with serious cyber capabilities.

COHOST: National policy is shifting from speed alone toward speed with guardrails, even if the guardrails are still being negotiated.

HOST: And Central Ohio should care because this region is absorbing the physical infrastructure costs of the AI buildout. Earlier this month, WOSU reported that AEP expects the total power it needs to generate by 2030 to nearly double, driven largely by data centers in Ohio and Texas. So the local version of the AI story is not abstract. It is about power demand, transmission buildout, rates, land use, and who pays when the national AI race arrives as concrete, wires, water, and higher utility pressure.

HOST: If Washington wants earlier visibility into powerful models, that may make policy sense. But it also underscores a tension this region keeps living with: the country wants more AI capacity, and places like Central Ohio are expected to host more of the infrastructure without having all the political leverage over the rules or the downstream costs. That is why this remains a live story rather than a niche tech story.

HOST: The markets snapshot this morning reflects most of those tensions at once. Stocks fell again on Tuesday. The Associated Press reports the S and P 500 dropped 49.44 points to 7,353.61, the Dow fell 322.24 points to 49,363.88, and the Nasdaq lost 220.02 points to 25,870.71. The driver was not one isolated company problem. It was higher yields, persistent inflation concern, and the sense that the market now has to price geopolitics and expensive money at the same time.

COHOST: And now Nvidia lands in the middle of that setup, which is why one earnings report suddenly feels like a stress test for the whole AI trade.

HOST: Reuters says options pricing implies Nvidia could swing by roughly 350 billion dollars in either direction after earnings today. That tells you how much pressure is sitting on one company to reassure investors that AI revenue momentum can still overpower higher rates, expensive valuations, and geopolitical instability. If Nvidia is great, it may steady sentiment. If it is merely good, that may not be enough in this market.

HOST: For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service says today will be a much different day from yesterday's heat. Showers are expected this morning, with showers and possibly a thunderstorm through early afternoon, and a high near 72. Then tonight turns mostly cloudy with a low around 48, and Thursday looks mostly sunny with a high near 70.

COHOST: So the practical weather note is easy today: cooler, wetter, and a lot less forgiving if you planned around yesterday's summer preview.

HOST: Earlier travel looks damp, the midday stretch still carries storm potential, and the bigger shift is the cooldown behind it. So if you are planning school pickups, outdoor work, or anything that depends on a stable window, today is more about avoiding rain gaps than beating heat.

HOST: The through line this morning is that several important stories are being tested by whether institutions can turn unstable headlines into stable policy. Iran is a test of whether a pause is real or just temporary hesitation. Taiwan is a test of whether deterrence gets restated clearly or left ambiguous. Senate Republicans are being tested on whether they can actually pass the package they keep revising. Columbus City Schools is being tested on whether it can protect student experience while shedding staff. The housing market is being tested on whether more listings matter if financing stays this expensive. AI policy is being tested on whether Washington can build oversight without pretending the infrastructure consequences happen somewhere else.

COHOST: And that leaves the watch list pretty clean for the rest of Wednesday.

HOST: Watch whether the White House offers any firmer language on Iran beyond tactical delay. Watch whether Taiwan gets any reassurance more concrete than yesterday's response from Taipei. Watch whether Senate Republicans narrow their package or keep exposing the gaps inside it. Watch whether the Massie result changes the tone of Republican dissent in the next few days. Watch how Columbus City Schools explains the operational effect of those cuts. Watch mortgage pricing, Treasury yields, and whether central Ohio buyers get any payment relief at all. Watch whether the White House actually releases that AI order this week. And watch Nvidia tonight, because one earnings report now carries far more symbolic weight than one company should probably have.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Wednesday, May 20th. Stay dry this morning, expect the cooler turn to hold, and keep an eye on the stories where the real question is no longer what leaders said, but whether any of it stabilizes.

Good morning. It is Tuesday, May 19th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The biggest pressure point sits where national security risk meets oil, inflation, and market nerves.

HOST: We begin with the story tying those threads together most directly. President Trump said Monday that he has put off a planned military strike on Iran that had been under consideration for today, Tuesday, May 19th, after Gulf allies asked for more time for negotiations. That takes the immediate edge off one scenario, but it does not settle the larger one.

HOST: The reason this remains the lead story is that the pause is tactical, not strategic. The Associated Press reported overnight that Trump described the delay as temporary and left open the possibility of renewed action if talks fail. Iran is still signaling distrust, and the Strait of Hormuz remains the central pressure point in the entire conflict. So this is not de-escalation you can bank on yet. It is a short extension on a crisis clock that is still running.

COHOST: And that is why this matters outside foreign policy circles. If the talks wobble again, oil, borrowing costs, and consumer nerves all feel it fast.

HOST: Almost every other beat in this brief keeps running through that same bottleneck. Oil moved lower from the most extreme levels after Trump's comments, but Reuters still described crude as roughly fifty percent above pre-war levels. Treasury yields have eased from Monday's highs, but they are still elevated enough to keep financing pressure on everything from home loans to growth stocks.

HOST: So the practical watch for today is simple. Are these talks real enough to keep military action off the table for more than another news cycle, or are markets and households just getting a brief pause before the next energy shock?

HOST: The second national story still carries continuity from yesterday, but the test has become even sharper. Taiwan is still trying to steady the fallout after Trump's comments following the Trump-Xi summit left open whether U.S. arms support might be treated more like a bargaining chip than a standing deterrent commitment. The Associated Press reported Sunday that President Lai Ching-te defended those arms purchases as the most important deterrent to regional conflict. That remains the essential response from Taipei this morning.

COHOST: What is fresh here is not a new White House clarification. It is the fact that one still has not arrived.

HOST: That absence is what keeps this story active. The longer the White House goes without clearly restating its Taiwan posture, the more room there is for allies, markets, and Beijing to read Trump's language as something more than improvisation. This is no longer mainly a summit optics story. It is a deterrence clarity story. If Washington wants to calm concerns, it has to say plainly whether the previously authorized Taiwan arms package is still moving on strategic terms rather than on transactional ones.

HOST: This also has a direct Ohio and Midwest angle. Taiwan risk runs through semiconductor supply, factory planning, freight insurance, corporate capex, and broader business confidence. When the signal from Washington gets fuzzy, the downstream effects are not limited to diplomats and defense analysts.

HOST: The third national story remains in the Senate, where Republicans are still trying to move a large immigration enforcement package through reconciliation while the parliamentarian keeps narrowing what survives. The latest visible setback remains the Associated Press report that a one billion dollar White House security proposal tied to the president's ballroom project does not qualify under Senate rules for inclusion in the bill as drafted.

COHOST: So this is becoming less a messaging story and more a discipline story.

HOST: That is the larger point. The more often leadership has to redraft, the more this stops being a story about broad Republican consensus on enforcement and becomes a story about whether they can build a bill disciplined enough to survive the procedural lane they chose. So this remains a proof-of-governance week. If Republicans stabilize the core bill, the story turns back toward implementation and spending scale. If they keep losing provisions, then the real headline becomes fragility, not momentum.

HOST: Back in Columbus, the lead local story still starts with Issue 5, but this morning the pressure is more administrative than political. Voters already delivered a decisive result. The city now has to show how that result becomes an operating model, and as of this morning there is still not a public-facing roadmap detailed enough to answer the practical questions residents should be asking.

COHOST: And those are not abstract questions anymore. Residents can reasonably ask who is in charge, what changes first, and when people will actually feel the difference.

HOST: Those questions remain largely unanswered in a concrete way. Who owns execution? What milestones will be public? How will dispatch rules change? What calls will shift away from a police-first response? How many people need to be hired, and on what timeline? What partner agencies are being relied on, and how will performance be measured?

HOST: The City of Columbus already has existing alternative crisis response programs in place, including Mobile Crisis Response and RREACT. That means the city is not building from zero. But Issue 5 was sold as a mandate to deepen and formalize a broader community crisis response system. Until City Hall shows the next-phase structure, the gap between voter approval and operational visibility stays wide.

HOST: That is why this story remains active for the tracker. The election is over, but the implementation clock is now the real story.

HOST: The second local story remains the housing ladder problem across Central Ohio, where the pressure is still visible at nearly every rung at once. WOSU reported last week that April closed sales in central Ohio fell 13.6 percent from a year earlier to 2,202, while the median sale price still reached 346,500 dollars. That is not a market collapse. It is a reminder that even with somewhat better inventory, affordability has not broken in the buyer's favor.

HOST: On the more urgent side of the same system, WOSU also reported that the annual point-in-time count found 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Columbus and Franklin County, including a sharp increase in the number of people living outside. Shelter use declined, but unsheltered homelessness rose from 455 to 651. Community Shelter Board leaders said they want to acquire three hotels to reduce pressure and create more flexible response capacity.

COHOST: This is one of those local stories where the fresh angle is the link between all the layers. The market story, the shelter story, and the affordability story are not separate anymore.

HOST: The continuity line here is still strong. Central Ohio is not dealing with one housing story. It is dealing with a chain reaction. High prices and high rates squeeze buyers. Limited deeply affordable options squeeze renters and fixed-income residents. That pushes more strain into shelters and eventually the unsheltered count. So the near-term watch remains whether local leaders move from diagnosis toward visible delivery through bond-backed housing announcements, movement on hotel acquisition, stronger homelessness response funding, or a clearer affordability pipeline.

HOST: On home lending and mortgage conditions, the gap between the weekly benchmark and the daily market is still the best way to understand what buyers are feeling. Freddie Mac's weekly survey for May 14 showed the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.36 percent, barely lower than the prior week. But Mortgage News Daily's daily index showed the 30-year fixed at 6.68 percent on Monday, May 18th, after another jump at the end of last week.

COHOST: That is the practical reality check. People may hear "rates are flat" and still experience financing as if it just got harder.

HOST: That gap matters because it explains why households can hear that rates are basically flat while lenders and buyers still feel financing stress intensifying in real time. The weekly average is slower. The daily market reacts faster to Treasury moves, oil-driven inflation worries, and general bond volatility. For Central Ohio buyers, the message is unchanged but more acute this morning. Some inventory is improving. Financing is not.

HOST: The AI and technology story this morning is still about governance catching up to capability. Axios reported Monday that more than sixty Trump allies are urging the White House to test and approve the most powerful AI models before they are broadly released. That adds pressure from inside Trump's broader political coalition to the concerns already coming from lawmakers and national security officials.

COHOST: And locally, this is not just a policy debate in Washington. It keeps landing in Central Ohio as power demand, water demand, and data center politics.

HOST: That matters because the AI buildout keeps arriving in Central Ohio not only as software ambition but as physical demand. WOSU reported this month that AEP expects to roughly double total power needs by 2030, largely because of data center demand in Ohio and Texas. Separate WOSU reporting also showed environmental groups pressing for tougher rules on new data centers because of their energy and water footprint.

HOST: So the national and local versions of this story are now clearly connected. Washington is arguing over model safety and oversight. Central Ohio is dealing with the infrastructure burden of the AI race itself. If the federal government wants more AI capacity, regions like this one keep getting asked to absorb more power load, more siting conflict, and more public concern about who pays.

HOST: The markets snapshot this morning reflects that same uneasy mix of caution and unresolved optimism. Reuters reported early Tuesday that U.S. stock futures were lower, with chip stocks under pressure and inflation worries still hanging over the market even as oil eased from Monday's peak and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped back to around 4.59 percent. On Monday, according to the Associated Press, the Dow gained 159.95 points to 49,686.12, while the S and P 500 fell 0.1 percent to 7,403.05 and the Nasdaq dropped 0.5 percent to 26,090.73.

COHOST: Investors still want the AI story, but they also have to price the cost of energy and money again.

HOST: That tells you what investors are trying to balance. There is still broad enthusiasm around AI earnings and semiconductor demand, but there is also a harder conversation about oil, inflation, bond yields, and whether tech valuations can hold up if money stays expensive. Nvidia earnings later this week matter because they are becoming a sentiment test for the whole AI trade at a moment when the macro background is getting less forgiving.

HOST: For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service says today, Tuesday, May 19th, will be mostly sunny and hot with a high near 90 degrees, followed by a 50 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon and a stronger chance of rain and storms tonight. Wednesday then turns cooler, with showers likely and a high near 73.

COHOST: So if you need the easier outdoor window, use the first half of the day and keep some flexibility for tonight.

HOST: The practical weather note is straightforward. The front half of the day is the heat story. The back half of the day and tonight are the storm story. If you need dry outdoor time, earlier is better. If you are planning around travel or events, keep the later weather turn in mind.

HOST: The through line this morning is that a lot of major stories are no longer being judged by what was announced. They are being judged by what holds. The Iran story is about whether a pause is durable enough to calm oil and inflation risk. The Taiwan story is about whether Washington restores deterrence clarity. The Senate story is about procedural survivability. Issue 5 is about building an actual system. Central Ohio housing is about whether affordability and homelessness pressure ease in any visible way. AI politics are about testing, control, infrastructure, and cost.

COHOST: And that gives you the watch list for the rest of the day: fewer ceremony stories, more follow-through stories.

HOST: So here is what to watch before this Tuesday turns into Wednesday. Watch whether the Iran negotiations produce anything more concrete than a short delay. Watch for any White House clarification on Taiwan arms support. Watch whether Senate Republicans can stop revising and start locking down their immigration package. Watch whether Columbus officials attach dates, staffing, or structure to Issue 5 implementation. Watch whether housing or homelessness leaders produce a visible delivery step rather than another diagnosis. Watch whether mortgage pricing settles after Monday's move to 6.68 percent on the daily index. Watch whether the White House signals where advanced AI testing will actually happen and under whose authority. Watch whether markets treat lower oil and slightly calmer yields as relief, or only as a brief breather before the next shock.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Tuesday, May 19th. Start early if you need the dry weather, stay flexible for the storms later, and keep an eye on the stories that are being tested by follow-through rather than headlines alone.

Good morning. It is Monday, May 18th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

We begin this morning with the story that remains the clearest measure of whether last week's Trump-Xi summit produced stability or simply postponed a harder argument. The newest turn is from Taipei, where Reuters reported overnight that Taiwan is now openly welcoming a direct call between President Trump and President Lai Ching-te as officials there try to calm the fallout from Trump's comments after the Beijing meeting.

That response matters because it confirms what we have been tracking since the summit closed. Taiwan heard Trump's remarks the same way markets, allies, and strategic planners heard them: as a signal that U.S. arms support may now be treated less like a standing deterrent and more like a negotiating variable. The Associated Press reported Sunday that Lai stressed U.S. arms purchases remain the most important deterrent to regional conflict and instability. In other words, Taiwan is trying to pull the conversation back to first principles before uncertainty hardens into a new policy baseline.

So the continuity line is sharper this morning. This is no longer just about diplomatic tone after a high-profile summit. It is about whether the United States is blurring a long-standing line around deterrence at the exact moment China wants more room to test that line. If Washington clarifies quickly, the damage may stay rhetorical. If it does not, then every market already sensitive to oil, shipping, semiconductors, and defense risk has another reason to stay nervous.

Why should listeners in Ohio care? Because Taiwan risk is not a remote abstraction. It runs through chip supply, manufacturing confidence, shipping insurance, energy pricing, and capital spending. If the post-summit message remains muddy, it becomes one more source of inflation pressure and one more excuse for markets to price in a harder path on rates.

The second national story is still in the Senate, where Republicans are trying to keep a broad immigration enforcement package alive while the parliamentarian keeps forcing rewrites. The Associated Press reported late Saturday that a proposal to include one billion dollars for White House security additions tied to the president's ballroom project failed Senate procedural rules and cannot stay in the package as drafted.

That does not end the bill, but it reinforces the same problem we talked about over the weekend. The narrower the reconciliation lane becomes, the harder it is to carry extra priorities inside it. Senate Republicans are still trying to move roughly seventy two billion dollars in immigration-related funding through a process that leaves very little room for anything that looks too broad, too incidental, or too loosely tied to budget rules.

The practical consequence is bigger than one rejected line item. Every forced revision eats time, narrows options, and exposes internal fault lines about what the party actually views as essential. If leadership keeps having to redraft, refine, and resubmit, then the story stops being just whether Republicans support tougher enforcement. It becomes whether they can write a bill disciplined enough to survive their own chosen procedure.

That makes this a real proof-phase week. Watch whether the Senate stabilizes the core of the package, or whether more provisions get stripped and the coalition begins to look thinner than advertised.

The third national story this morning is not a brand-new headline, but it is still an active piece of the wider political map. The Supreme Court's decision late last week preserved access to mifepristone while the legal fight continues, so the immediate disruption to patients and providers has been avoided for now. The practical reality remains that women can still get the medication by mail and through pharmacies without a required in-person doctor visit while the appeal moves forward.

The reason it still belongs in the brief is that the calm is operational, not final. The underlying fight over how far courts can reach into long-settled FDA decisions is still alive, and it remains one of the clearest examples of how legal risk can keep hanging over national policy even after an immediate cliff has been moved back. The short-term situation stabilized. The long-term precedent is still unresolved.

Back here in Columbus, the biggest local story remains Issue 5, but the framing changes a little on a Monday because this is no longer a campaign story at all. Columbus City Council is back in session today, and the city enters another civic work week with voters having already delivered a clear verdict. The question now is not whether the charter amendment had support. The question is whether the city can show actual implementation structure for the expanded community crisis response system.

That means the same operational questions still define the story. Who owns execution inside city government? What milestones will be public? How will dispatch rules change? Which calls move away from a police-first posture? What hiring timeline exists? What clinical and nonprofit partnerships are actually being built? And when should residents expect to see something more concrete than general language about commitment and progress?

The reason to keep this story hot is simple. A seventy-seven percent vote share settles legitimacy, but it does not settle administration. Columbus now owes residents a visible implementation path, and every meeting week that begins without that path becoming clearer raises the odds that the city drifts from mandate into muddle.

The second local story is still the full housing ladder problem in Central Ohio. WOSU's latest housing reporting showed April closed sales down 13.6 percent from a year ago to 2,202, even as inventory improved. That might sound like some market cooling, but the median price still hit 346,500 dollars. So the region may be getting a little more selection, but affordability has not meaningfully broken in favor of buyers.

And that is only the upper-middle rung of the ladder. On the harder edge of the same problem, WOSU's homelessness reporting this month showed 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Columbus and Franklin County, with a notable rise in people living outside even as shelter use fell. Community Shelter Board leaders said they want to acquire three hotels to relieve pressure, and city officials have already acknowledged that the added 7.2 million dollars in the budget is not enough by itself.

That is why the continuity line still matters. Central Ohio is not just experiencing a housing market that feels expensive. It is experiencing a system where pressure is visible at every level at once. Buyers face high prices and high borrowing costs. Renters face scarce affordable units. Service systems face stronger shelter strain. And the unsheltered count says some people are simply being pushed all the way out of the formal market.

So the next five-day watch is not abstract. Do local officials connect the positive-sounding inventory story to any visible action on affordability, shelter capacity, hotel acquisition, or the bond-funded housing pipeline? If not, then the region is still mostly describing the pressure rather than relieving it.

On home lending and mortgages, the official weekly benchmark remains Freddie Mac's May 14 survey, which showed the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.36 percent, barely down from 6.37 percent the prior week. Technically that is an improvement. In real household terms, it is still a heavy financing environment.

More importantly, the daily market has been less friendly than the weekly average suggests. Mortgage News Daily's rate index ended Friday at 6.65 percent for a top-tier 30-year fixed loan, up sharply as bond yields climbed. That difference is worth explaining because it tells the real story. Freddie Mac gives the slower-moving weekly average based on completed application data. Mortgage News Daily gives a more immediate view of lender pricing as rate markets swing. Put them together, and the message is consistent: the mortgage market is not improving in a durable way yet. It is wobbling around an elevated baseline.

For Central Ohio, that matters because even a modest local increase in inventory does not help much if financing costs keep offsetting it. More people can look. Fewer can comfortably act. That is why affordability still feels frozen even when some of the headline supply numbers appear to be softening in the right direction.

The AI and technology story this morning is a useful reminder that Washington is still arguing with itself about whether advanced models should mainly be accelerated, tested, restricted, or all three. Axios reported overnight that more than sixty Trump allies, including Steve Bannon and other prominent MAGA figures, are pressing the White House to test and approve the most powerful AI models before they are broadly released.

That is politically notable because it widens the pressure beyond the bipartisan lawmaker concerns we were already watching last week. Until now, a lot of the argument around frontier AI oversight looked like a fight between cyber officials, industry, and some members of Congress. This new letter suggests part of Trump's own coalition is also moving toward the view that the government cannot stay mostly hands-off once models become powerful enough to discover vulnerabilities at scale or automate more offensive cyber work.

The real issue underneath the politics is still capability. Advanced models are already strong enough to force a live policy debate about access, testing, classification, and pre-release review. The government has not settled who should run those tests, how broad they should be, or where speed should give way to caution. That leaves the White House trying to defend innovation while also responding to a growing number of people who think the cyber risks are arriving faster than the institutions meant to manage them.

And, again, there is a direct Columbus angle. The AI boom does not only arrive as software. It arrives as infrastructure. Data centers, power demand, water demand, grid upgrades, semiconductor supply chains, and local siting fights are part of the same national push. The policy argument in Washington may sound ideological, but the local version is concrete: if the country wants more AI capacity, places like Central Ohio keep getting asked to absorb more of the physical footprint.

That is a blunt phrase, and it matters because it sharpens the continuity line we have been tracking since the summit began. The issue is not whether Washington and Beijing can stage a calmer tone for a few days. The issue is whether core strategic commitments are becoming bargaining material.

Taiwan has always been the live wire in this relationship, and China made that clear again during the summit. That leaves allies, markets, and military planners with the same immediate question: is this temporary negotiation language, or is it a sign that deterrence itself is being repriced?

Why does that matter to listeners far from Washington and Beijing? Because unresolved Taiwan risk does not stay neatly inside foreign policy. It runs straight into shipping routes, semiconductor supply chains, energy nerves, defense spending, and investor confidence. If that uncertainty grows, then oil stays sensitive, inflation stays harder to cool, and borrowing costs stay heavier than households want them to be.

So this is still the same summit aftermath story, but the framing is more serious this morning. Last week we were asking whether the visit would produce proof instead of theater. Today the proof test is even simpler. Do tensions actually cool, or did the trip just make clearer which pressure points remain available for leverage.

The second national story is still on the Senate side, where the immigration enforcement package we have been following is now looking even more procedurally fragile. The Associated Press reported late Saturday that the Senate parliamentarian ruled against a proposal to include one billion dollars for White House security additions and the president's ballroom project inside the broader Republican bill for immigration enforcement agencies.

That ruling does not kill the whole package, but it adds to the larger pattern that was already visible on Friday. Republicans are trying to move a roughly seventy two billion dollar bill through a narrow reconciliation path, and the parliamentarian keeps reminding them that the path is in fact narrow. Every provision that gets knocked out or rewritten increases the time pressure, the drafting pressure, and the political pressure.

It is becoming a test of whether Senate Republicans can separate what is core from what is ornamental, keep the coalition together, and survive the procedural gauntlet without losing momentum before committee work and floor planning get tighter.

If leadership has to keep trimming and restructuring, then disagreements about cost, scope, and side priorities become much harder to hide.

National story number three is a legal and institutional fight that remains highly relevant even without a fresh overnight turn. The longer term question about how aggressively courts can second guess the Food and Drug Administration after years of regulation is still unresolved. So the right read this morning is that disruption was delayed, not that the institutional fight is over.

Roll Call reports that Senate Republicans have now put legislative text behind a roughly 69.2 billion dollar enforcement package, including about 39.2 billion dollars from the Judiciary Committee side and roughly 26 billion dollars for Customs and Border Protection. We flagged this yesterday as a move from message politics into governing detail, and that is still the right frame.

Once the text is public, this stops being a generic border argument and becomes a concrete fight over detention capacity, staffing, technology, transport, and fiscal priorities. It also becomes a test of whether Republicans can keep internal unity around a very large enforcement expansion while the public is still focused on affordability. Watch for procedural attacks from Democrats, but also watch for whether cost concerns inside the GOP become louder now that the real numbers are on paper.

Back here in Columbus, the biggest continuity story remains the emergency response charter amendment that voters approved by a landslide on Tuesday, May 5. Axios Columbus reported that Issue 5 passed with 77 percent support and sets up a path toward round-the-clock non-police response options for some nonviolent 911 calls, with rollout goals beginning in 2028 and fuller implementation by 2030.

The political campaign is over. The hard part starts now. This is where implementation stories get won or lost. The questions are no longer whether voters liked the idea. The questions are who owns the rollout, how dispatch criteria are defined, how quickly staffing plans are built, how funding scales over time, and whether City Hall keeps public momentum alive now that the ballot energy is gone.

That shift matters because Issue 5 passed so decisively that a weak follow-through would stand out immediately. Big margins create big expectations. So over the next several days, listen for early signs of administrative seriousness. If city leaders start naming timelines, leadership structure, and near-term milestones, the story will feel durable. If the post-election message gets vague, skepticism will return quickly.

Another Columbus story we are still tracking is the aftermath of the Jason Meade verdict in the Casey Goodson Jr. case. Axios Columbus noted Monday that the reckless homicide conviction is unusual for an officer-involved shooting case, but it also leaves a major unresolved question because the jury did not agree on the murder charge. That means the case produced accountability, but not full closure.

That distinction is important. A conviction changes the conversation, but it does not end it. The next thing to watch is whether prosecutors say anything soon about retrying the unresolved count, or whether the legal system effectively signals that the reckless homicide verdict is where this story will end before July sentencing. Either answer would carry civic weight in Columbus, because this case has always been about more than one courtroom result. It has also been about public trust.

The broader housing pressure story in Franklin County is still active too. Axios Columbus reported last week that the latest point-in-time count reached a record 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Franklin County, the fourth straight annual high. Even though that report is not brand new this morning, it remains one of the most important local trend lines because it is unlikely to leave the agenda quickly.

The reason to keep it active is that it sharpens the local policy test. Columbus is talking about public safety reform, major development, and infrastructure demands tied to growth, but the affordability crisis is still getting worse at the household level. Record homelessness means the housing debate is no longer abstract. If leaders respond, the signs will likely show up in shelter capacity, supportive housing commitments, or a more urgent public framing from city and county officials. If they do not, this data point will keep hanging over every growth narrative in the region.

On home lending and mortgage rates, the newest benchmark still comes from Freddie Mac's survey released Thursday, May 7. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.37 percent, up from 6.30 percent the prior week. Realtor.com said rising rates and geopolitical uncertainty made both buyers and sellers more cautious at the start of the spring market, while Axios Columbus reported earlier that Central Ohio sales have been shifting more toward the suburbs as Franklin County affordability stays tight.

That combination tells the story this way: conditions are not collapsing, but relief is limited. Inventory is somewhat better than it was in the tightest years, yet borrowing costs remain high enough to keep many households cautious. And because oil is back above 100 dollars and Treasury yields moved up again Monday, the mortgage story remains connected to the same global pressure we opened with.

For listeners in Central Ohio, that means the spring market is still a math problem before it is an optimism problem. A slightly better selection of homes helps, but not enough to outweigh the payment shock many buyers still face. If rates stay lodged in the mid-sixes, affordability pressure remains the main headline even if the market keeps moving.

In AI and technology, the current phase of competition keeps looking less like a race for the flashiest demo and more like a race for deployment, security review, and infrastructure capacity. Reuters reported last week that Microsoft, Google, and xAI agreed to give the U.S. government early access to frontier models for national security testing, extending a broader shift toward pre-release evaluation. Reuters also reported last week that AI services and deployment expertise are becoming valuable enough that major model companies are trying to buy their way deeper into enterprise implementation.

That matters because it reinforces the same idea we have been tracking: the AI economy is maturing from novelty toward systems. The real contest is increasingly about who can place tools inside big institutions, who can clear security concerns, who can supply enough compute, and who can sustain the physical infrastructure underneath all of it.

That national AI story still has a Columbus angle. Axios Columbus reported last week that local leaders are exploring the use of reclaimed wastewater to cool data centers, precisely because the region's growth in digital infrastructure is now colliding with real resource constraints. So when people talk about AI as an infrastructure build-out, Central Ohio is not observing that from a distance. It is living part of it directly.

The markets snapshot this morning is a mix of strength and caution. According to Reuters and the Associated Press, the S and P 500 closed Monday at 7,412.84, the Nasdaq at 26,274.13, and the Dow at 49,704.47. The S and P and Nasdaq both finished at record highs again, which tells you investors are still willing to stay with growth and AI-linked momentum even while oil rises.

But the caution part matters just as much. Reuters reported that the 10-year Treasury yield moved up to about 4.41 percent on Monday as oil stoked fresh inflation concern. That is the market saying higher energy costs still have the power to complicate the soft-landing narrative. Stocks can celebrate strong momentum and still admit that the cost of capital may not come down as quickly as bulls want.

So the best way to read markets this morning is not simple optimism. It is selective confidence. Investors are still rewarding earnings strength, AI demand, and large-cap resilience. But they are also re-pricing oil risk in real time, and that means the macro backdrop is less comfortable than the record closes alone would suggest.

For Columbus weather, the latest available National Weather Service forecast for Columbus calls for a mostly sunny Tuesday with a high near 64, then showers likely Tuesday night with a low around 49. Wednesday stays unsettled, with a chance of showers and a high near 68.

So the practical weather note is easy today. Use the dry window while you have it, because the cleaner part of the forecast is daytime Tuesday, and conditions look wetter heading into tonight and Wednesday.

The through-line this morning is that almost every major story is demanding proof, not promises. Diplomacy around Iran only matters if shipping risk actually improves. The Supreme Court's temporary abortion-pill order only delays a disruptive answer until at least Thursday, May 14. Senate Republicans now have real immigration numbers on paper, so the fiscal and procedural fight gets sharper. Columbus voters approved a new emergency-response structure, so implementation now becomes the real test. The Meade verdict created accountability without final civic closure. Record homelessness keeps insisting that growth without affordability is not enough. Mortgage rates remain high enough to dominate the housing conversation. And AI's future keeps looking more physical, regulated, and resource-intensive than purely digital.

So watch these points today: any concrete sign of safer shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, any signal from the Supreme Court beyond its Thursday mifepristone deadline, any procedural movement on the Senate enforcement package, any specific implementation language out of Columbus on Issue 5, any prosecutorial signal in the Goodson case, any stronger local response to the homelessness data, whether bond yields keep firming with oil, and whether the AI story keeps broadening from software into infrastructure and governance.

That is your Morning Brief for Tuesday, May 12th. Have a good morning, make use of the dry stretch before the rain comes back tonight, and keep your eye on the stories that now have to prove they are moving in the real world.
